newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine Nov inflation seen at 5.7 pct-poll.
newsitem.headline: Philippine Nov inflation seen at 5.7 pct-poll.

text.p: Philippine inflation is expected to rise to 5.7 percent in November from 4.7 in October due to higher spending for the Christmas season and the impact of a recent increase in transportation fares, a Reuter poll showed.

The average 5.7 percent figure yielded by the poll of five financial institutions completed on Tuesday showed year-on-year inflation in November would be much lower that the year-ago 11.1 percent when a rice shortage had sent prices soaring.
The government, which last week forecast the figure at 6.0 to 6.3 percent, is scheduled to announce November inflation on Thursday.
"We're assuming a month-on-month change of 0.75 to 1.0 percentage point," said Dennis Lapid, an economist of Vickers Ballas Securities.

Economists said their forecasts were generally lower than the government because it assumed the half-month impact of an increase in transportation fares and a delay in the monthly adjustments in domestic oil prices.
"The full impact of the transportation hike is one percentage point. But only half of that will be reflected in November," said economist Lito Dalit of AsianBank Corp.
Effective last November 14, bus fares were increased by 14 to 33 percent by the government's Land Transportation Franchising & Regulatory Board.

The fare increases were granted after the government raised domestic fuel prices in three successive months due to the implementation of a new oil pricing scheme that would pave the way for the full deregulation of the petroleum industry by March 1997. The new scheme was computed based on Singapore posted oil prices.

On Tuesday, the Philippines' Energy Regulatory Board chairman Bayani Faylona told Reuters that prices of most petroleum products would be again raised by 50 centavos per litre. The adjustments will be announced at a news conference at 12 noon (0400 GMT) on Tuesday, he said.
The decision to raise prices comes after a month's delay when the adjustments were put on hold because of a complaint by a Congressman that they were unjustified.
"The delay in the oil price hike had effectively placed the clamour for higher wages out of the picture in the near term," said Paul Joseph Garcia, an economist of Metrobank.
Inflation currently is being driven by cost-push concerns, and not by money supply factors, the analysts said.
The Central Bank had reported that base money, a measure of domestic liquidity slowed to a year-on-year growth of 7.6 percent in November from 13.2 in the previous month.
Moreover, analysts said the peso was stable at an average of 26.266 in November from 26.27 in October.
For the entire year 1996, economists expected the average inflation rate at 8.7 percent in line with the government's target.

The 1996 forecast is higher than the 1995 average of 8.1 percent due to the effect of severe rice shortages, which sent inflation to a year-high of 11.8 percent in February. Inflation tapered off to single digit in June until it bottomed out at 4.4 percent in September.
Following are the forecasts made by five financial institutions (in percentage terms):
Nov Full-year 1996
AsianBank 5.8 8.7
F.Yap Securities 5.8-6.4 8.7-8.8
Metrobank 5.5-6.0 8.8
SBC Warburg 5.1 8.6
Vickers Ballas Securities 5.5-5.8 8.8
